extracted.intended_audience: artists, art students, and critics interested in landscape painting and visual truth (readers of Ruskin/19th‑century art theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative criteria for creating and judging landscape painting (truth, tone, color, space, skies, clouds, execution and the ideas conveyable by art). A 19th‑century art‑critical framework emphasizing truthful representation and modes of execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion no criterion of excellence, except after long periods of time
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion no criterion of excellence, except after long periods of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public taste is not a reliable immediate test of artistic excellence; only over long historical periods does public opinion approximate true judgment. Related notes: public opinion becomes obstinate when formed; it should be opposed only on points capable of demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between the painter's intellectual power and technical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between the painter's intellectual power and technical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greatness in art requires both intellectual/expressive power and technical facility, which are distinct qualities. The critic should distinguish language/thought expressed by the painter from merely technical accomplishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting, as such, is nothing more than language
rubrics_metrics.description: "Painting, as such, is nothing more than language."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat painting as a form of language: its elements (composition, tone, color, form) function like words or syntax conveying ideas. This perspective frames evaluative criteria in terms of clarity, expressiveness, and appropriateness of visual 'speech.'

rubrics_metrics.name: "Painter" corresponds to "versifier" (role-based definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Painter,' a term corresponding to 'versifier.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'painter' can be used analytically like 'versifier'—distinguishing between mere surface craft and genuine expressive content. Use such distinctions when judging works that prioritize technical surface over meaningful expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas conveyable by art: classes of conveyable ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: What classes of ideas are conveyable by art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art can convey various classes of ideas (developed elsewhere as power, imitation, truth, beauty, relation). Evaluate works by which class of idea they successfully convey and the relative dignity of those ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of power: relative dignity and source
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of power vary much in relative dignity; they are received from whatever has been the subject of power. The meaning of the word 'excellence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing 'power' in art, consider the source and dignity of the idea (higher subjects yield higher ideas of power). The pleasure from conquering difficulties is legitimate; however, avidity for mere power can lead to low choices. Execution must support true power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of imitation: imitation as contemptible when easy
rubrics_metrics.description: False use of the term 'imitation' by many writers on art; real meaning of the term; imitation is only of contemptible subjects; imitation is contemptible because it is easy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation (mere copying) is low on the scale of artistic ideas — it yields contemptible pleasure because it is easy. Evaluate negatively works that prioritize simple imitation over truthful or powerful invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of truth distinguished from imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaning of the word 'truth' as applied to art; differences between truth and imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth in art is not the same as mere imitation. Truth involves rendering characteristic, particular, and significant facts of nature or idea; it should be valued higher than facile resemblance or generalized formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of beauty and taste: definition and intellectual rank
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition of the term 'beautiful.' Definition of the term 'taste.' Distinction between taste and judgment. How far beauty may become intellectual. The high rank and function of ideas of beauty; meaning of 'ideal beauty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate beauty both sensorially and intellectually: 'taste' differs from critical judgment. Consider whether beauty in a work attains an ideal/intellectual level rather than mere superficial prettiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of relation: breadth and nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: General meaning of the term 'relation'; which ideas are to be comprehended under it; the exceeding nobility of these ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge compositions on their relational ideas (composition of parts, associations, narrative or symbolic relations). Such ideas are noble and do not require fine subdivisions — consider overall relational effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: No necessity for detailed separate study of imitation or power except under one form
rubrics_metrics.description: No necessity for detailed study of ideas of imitation or separate study of ideas of power, except under one particular form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical focus should be selective: only under particular conditions does separate analysis of imitation or power yield insight; otherwise consider them within broader categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two inconsistent modes of receiving ideas of power
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two modes of receiving ideas of power, commonly inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize both modes and the reasons for their inconsistency; the sensation of power ought not to be sought in imperfect art. Evaluate whether a work confuses or contradicts these modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of execution that produce ideas of power
rubrics_metrics.description: The first quality of execution is truth; the second, simplicity; the third, mystery; the fourth, inadequacy; and the fifth, decision; the sixth, velocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging execution, look for these qualities in order: truth (accuracy/faithfulness to the idea), simplicity (clarity), mystery (depth/suggestion), inadequacy (deliberate understatement), decision (resoluteness of handling), velocity (sense of energetic execution). Note that these sources of pleasure can be inconsistent with one another and with other aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strangeness is an illegitimate source of pleasure in execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Strangeness an illegitimate source of pleasure in execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid valuing mere novelty or oddity for its own sake; judge strangeness critically—only legitimate sources of pleasure in execution should be praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fondness for ideas of power may lead to lowest choices; peril of pursuing power alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Fondness for ideas of power leads to the adoption of the lowest. Therefore perilous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of artists who pursue power without moral/aesthetic discrimination: this can result in coarse or base subject choices. Evaluate whether pursuit of 'power' is grounded in dignified material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity defined: effect upon the mind of anything above it
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity is the effect upon the mind of anything above it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess 'sublime' works by whether they genuinely elevate the mind (not merely arouse fear). The highest beauty is sublime; the critic should test whether elevation (not just danger) is produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two great ends of landscape painting: representation of facts and thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: The two great ends of landscape painting are the representation of facts and thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landscape painters should aim at (a) truthful representation of natural fact and (b) conveyance of thought/feeling. These ends induce different material selection: facts favor sameness; thoughts require variety. Both are valuable, but have different audiences and duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of nature not discerned by uneducated senses
rubrics_metrics.description: The common self-deception of men with respect to their power of discerning truth; men usually see little of what is before their eyes; sight depends upon previous knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and artists must recognize that perception must be trained. Evaluate claims to 'truth' by considering the observer's level of training and moral/intellectual sensibility; untrained senses often miss essential natural truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative importance of truths: particular truths over general ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessity of determining the relative importance of truths. Falseness of the maxim that general truths are more important than particular ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value particular, characteristic truths (species-level details) when they are significant; general truths in the subject-matter can be important, but particularity in the predicate gives value. Evaluate works by the characteristic truthfulness of particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative importance of truths: rare truths over frequent ones
rubrics_metrics.description: No accidental violation of nature's principles should be represented. But the cases in which those principles have been strikingly exemplified, which are comparatively rare, are of greater importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer representation of striking, less common natural truths rather than repeated commonplace facts; repetition is blameable. Judge subject selection for rarity/importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative importance of truths: truths of colour least important
rubrics_metrics.description: Color is a secondary quality, therefore less important than form; color no distinction between objects of the same species; form (explained by light and shade) is primary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating landscape, prioritize form, light and shade (chiaroscuro) over color alone. Color is context-dependent and less definitive of species or character; do not judge truthfulness solely by chromatic fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of historical truths; form via light and shade primary
rubrics_metrics.description: Recapitulation: The importance of historical truths. Form, as explained by light and shade, the first of all truths. Tone, light, and color are secondary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical/characteristic truth (how things are in context and over time) is vital. Emphasize form and chiaroscuro over superficial coloristic effects when judging authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: General application: different selection of facts for imitation vs truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The different selection of facts consequent on the several aims at imitation or at truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine an artist's aim (imitation vs truth) to judge selection of material. Old masters often aimed at imitation; modern artists often aim at truth and variety — evaluate choices accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish and the right/ wrong use of finish
rubrics_metrics.description: Finish, and the want of it, how right--and how wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finish (level of completion/detail) can be appropriate or inappropriate depending on aim: finish is necessary for certain expressions of truth (particularly in landscape foregrounds), but overfinish or misplaced finish can be wrong. Judge degree of finish relative to subject and intended truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: The excellence of skies: open sky qualities and truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature and essential qualities of the open blue; its connection with clouds; its exceeding depth. Many ideas of sky are conventional; best skies of ancients are inimitable in quality but childish in rendering various truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess skies by their truthful depth, relation to cloud, and subtle phenomena (sunbeams, vapor). Avoid conventional clichés; value accurate perception of delicate atmospheric phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of clouds: study of three regions (cirrus, central, rain-cloud)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cloud character varies by elevation; three regions (upper/cirrus, central, rain-cloud) each have distinct truths in form, color, transparency and scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge cloud-painting by accurate typology: upper cirrus delicacy/quantity/color, central cumulus monumental forms/infinity, and low rain-clouds for proximity, color, and transient effects. The multiplicity, scale, transparency and infinity of clouds are key tests of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of infinity as a test of all truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasons for insisting on the infinity of Turner's works. Infinity is almost an unerring test of all truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work conveys a sense of infinity/limitlessness where appropriate; absence of this quality can indicate falsehood or novice multiplication of objects. Use 'infinity' as a heuristic for authenticity of atmospheric/space rendering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of tone: relation of middle tints, qualities of light
rubrics_metrics.description: Meanings of 'tone'—(1) right relation of objects in shadow to the principal light; (2) quality of color by which it is felt to owe part of its brightness to the hue of light upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tone both in structural relation to light/dark and in coloristic quality influenced by light. Examine middle tints relative to principal light and darkness; assess compositional tone unifying the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of color: limitations and Turner's approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations that painters (even Turner) are often inferior in brilliancy to nature; necessary discrepancy exists between attainable brilliancy of color and light; Turner's translation of colors and basis of gray under vivid hues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge color with awareness of natural brilliancy limits and the relation between color and light; appreciate color systems that subordinate chroma to tonal and chiaroscural truth rather than seek pure vividness alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of chiaroscuro: distinction of shadows and lights
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinctness of shadows is the chief means of expressing vividness of light. Second principle: both high light and deep shadow are used in equal quantity, and only in points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate use of chiaroscuro for truthful expression: clear, decisive contrasts in appropriate points express nature's lights; avoid systems that blur or ignore middle/dark/bright relationships. Students are often misled by older systems—critique accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of space: drawing and focus of the eye
rubrics_metrics.description: Space is more clearly indicated by the drawing of objects than by their hue. It is impossible to see objects at unequal distances distinctly at one moment; in painting either foreground or distance must be partially sacrificed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess spatial truth by drawing and selective focus: modern artists succeed by sacrificing some detail to convey depth. Evaluate whether foreground/distance handling creates believable space rather than equal distinctness or vacancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of space: power of the eye and indistinctness with distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Peculiar indistinctness dependent on the retirement of objects from the eye; two great resultant truths: nature is never distinct, and never vacant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge landscapes for appropriate loss of detail with distance and against false vacancy; fullness and finish are especially necessary in landscape foregrounds. Evaluate breadth vs vacancy carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish is more necessary in landscape than in historical subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Finish is far more necessary in landscape than in historical subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating landscapes, expect higher degree of finish/fulness of detail than might be required in historical painting; judge if execution achieves that necessary fulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of light rendered by modern art: studied phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern artists render particular effects of light (not exhaustively examined here), and further investigation is hoped for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a painter's treatment of special light effects (sunbeams, mist, rainlight) as a distinct criterion; attention to such phenomena signals depth of observation and truthfulness.
